sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section provides the header and date for the maamar delivered on Motzaei Simchat Torah 5738.

translations.translation: B”SD.
Motzaei Simchat Torah – in his room – 5738

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the joy of Simchat Torah is expressed specifically through dancing with a covered Torah scroll, accessible to all Jews including the simplest, and that even one who does not understand draws down Ein Sof to Atzmus.

translations.translation: To understand the concept of Simchat Torah,
and the precise point is known regarding this,
that the manner of the joy
(of Simchat Torah)
is that they take a Torah scroll as it is rolled up and covered with a mantle,
and dance with it.
For despite that it is written in the Torah
that it is “your wisdom and your understanding,” etc., nevertheless, this manner of joy is not through study and contemplation, but specifically through dancing.
Therefore, the joy of Simchat Torah is for all of Israel,
even for the most simple who have no connection to comprehension and understanding,
[and furthermore,
that during the joy and dances of the hakafot, there are drawn
(werden tzugezoygn)
also those who during the rest of the year the connection and unity of their
[matters of]
Torah is not apparent,
as is seen tangibly].
And this concept
(that the joy of Simchat Torah is in every Jew)
is also expressed in that they dance specifically with a Torah scroll—the Written Torah—
for even one who does not know what is being said recites the blessing over the Torah when reading from the Written Torah.
And since that which he recites the blessing over the Torah is by the command of the Torah of truth,
it is simple that this is indeed the reality,
that even one who does not know what is being said draws down Ein Sof to Atzmus and Essence
(the Giver of the Torah)
into the Torah that he learns.
It is also known
the precise point: why do they celebrate Simchat Torah on Shemini Atzeret
(and in the diaspora on the second day of Shemini Atzeret),
for seemingly it should be on Shavuot, the time of the giving of our Torah.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the reason for Simchat Torah on Shemini Atzeret through the Midrashic parable of the king and his daughters, where Yom Kippur is the “one day” all gather, and Shemini Atzeret/Simchat Torah is the “one festival” of rejoicing together.

translations.translation: B)
And the explanation of this is brought
based on what is stated in the Midrash:

“The Atzeret of the festival [of Sukkot] was fitting to be fifty days distant, corresponding to the Atzeret of Pesach, but the Atzeret of the festival, because they are going from summer to winter, the days are not sufficient for them to go and come.
A parable: to what is this comparable? To a king who had many daughters,
some married to a nearby place and some married to a distant place.
One day they all came to inquire as to the welfare of the king, their father.
The king said: These who are married to a nearby place, it is possible for them to go and come,
but those who are married to a distant place, it is not possible for them to go and come.
Until they are all here with me, let us all make one festival and rejoice with them.
So too, the Atzeret of Pesach, while they are going from winter to summer, the Holy One, blessed be He, said: It is possible for them to go and come.

But the Atzeret of the festival, because they are going from summer to winter, etc., the Holy One, blessed be He, said: It is not possible for them to go and come. Rather, until they are here, let us all make one festival and rejoice.”
And this is why they celebrate Simchat Torah on Shemini Atzeret,
for the “one day” on which all the daughters come
[the daughters of Zion and Jerusalem,
that is, the souls of Israel]
to inquire as to the welfare of the king, their father, refers
to Yom Kippur,
and afterwards He says, “Let us all make one festival and rejoice,”
this is
Simchat Torah
(which is established on Shemini Atzeret),
which is “one festival” analogous to the “one day” of Yom Kippur.
